content: 1. Immunization, growth, development, care-seeking, and illness management are critical aspects of maternal and child health. However, barriers exist in engaging parents with web-based health record systems, such as the eRedBook, due to the absence of a health education component and challenges in recruitment by health visitors. 2. A qualitative study by Phipps (2001) involved face-to-face interviews with 21 English-speaking pregnant women in their second or third trimester who had attended antenatal clinics in Australia at least twice. The study explored the use of women-held antenatal care (ANC) cards, which allowed women to carry their medical records throughout pregnancy, fostering a sense of patient control, participation in decision-making, and improved communication with healthcare providers. However, unintended negative consequences of paper-based records were noted, as they lacked a health education component and had a single focus. 3. Quinlivan, Lyons, and Peterson (2014) conducted a mixed-methods study involving surveys with 474 obstetric patients in Australia. The study examined attitudes toward personally controlled electronic health record (PCEHR) systems, which consolidate information from multiple sources into a single secure record. While antenatal patients preferred the PCEHR system for its perceived benefits, concerns were raised about its comparison to hospital-based or patient-held paper records. The web-based system was single-focused and lacked a health education component. 4. Sharp et al. (2014) conducted a mixed-methods study involving semi-structured interviews with childhood cancer survivors (n=4), caregivers (n=11), and survivor-caregiver dyads (n=5) in the USA. The study explored the use of electronic personal health records (ePHRs) for pediatric cancer survivors, which are secure, internet-accessible records managed by the survivor. Participants expressed interest in and positive attitudes toward ePHRs, although the system was single-focused and lacked a health education component. 5. Yanagisawa et al. (2015) conducted a mixed-methods study in Cambodia, involving interviews with 20 multiparous women, 8 midwives and nurses, and 10 village health volunteers and traditional birth attendants. The study evaluated the Maternal and Child Health (MCH) Handbook, a paper-based record that included information on pregnancy, delivery, postpartum health, child growth and development, immunization, and dental health. The handbook was culturally appropriate and included a health education component, but potential obstacles and side effects of its implementation were identified. 6. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued 12 recommendations on home-based records (HBRs) for maternal, newborn, and child health. These recommendations emphasize the importance of multi-focus records with health education components to improve health outcomes. 7. Studies such as those by Byczkowski et al. (2014) and Clendon and Dignam (2010) have highlighted the usability and value of web-based patient portals and child health record books in fostering relationships between healthcare providers and families. These tools have been shown to improve communication, health-related behaviors, and perceptions of care quality. 8. Research by Hagiwara et al. (2013) in Palestine demonstrated that the MCH Handbook effectively improved health-related behaviors. Similarly, Yanagisawa et al. (2015) found that the handbook increased maternal knowledge and behavior in rural Cambodia. 9. Various international studies have explored the design, implementation, and impact of home-based records. For example, the development of a combined maternal and child health record book in Ghana (Hagiwara, 2017) and the use of MCH booklets for refugees in Jordan (Kanda, 2017) have been documented as successful initiatives. 10. The WHO, UNICEF, and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation have organized workshops to revitalize home-based records in countries such as Ethiopia, Liberia, and Madagascar. These efforts aim to address challenges in record retention, perceived usefulness, and implementation. 11. Studies have also examined the role of digital tools, such as apps for refugee populations in Jordan, to enhance access to child health information (Kanda, 2017). These tools aim to integrate health education and improve usability for diverse populations. 12. The WHO Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health has compiled a comprehensive report on the facilitators and barriers to the appropriate use of home-based records. This report draws on experiences from multiple countries and highlights the importance of multi-focus records with integrated health education components.
